title: India sold a record $89.99 billion abroad in October, but the gap on goods grew
subtitle: Exports of goods and services reached an all-time monthly high, while costly oil pushed the import bill for goods to a record too.
content_html:
Picture India as one giant shop. In October 2026, this shop sold more to the world than in any month before. On Friday, 13 November 2026, the commerce ministry said India's total exports, goods and services together, reached $89.99 billion in October 2026, up 29.90% from October 2025. But the same shop also bought a record amount from abroad. So the gap on goods alone grew to $39.88 billion, the biggest in a year.

Both things are true in the same month. Here is what the numbers mean, in simple words.

First, what are exports and imports?

An export is something made or done in India and sold to a buyer in another country. A shirt from Tiruppur sold in London is an export. So is software written in Chennai for a bank in New York. That second one is a service: work you cannot drop on your foot.

An import works the other way round. It is something India buys from another country, like crude oil from Russia or phone parts made in China.

Think of your pocket money. Exports are the money coming in. Imports are the money going out.

A record month for selling to the world

The ministry's own release gives the full picture. Total exports rose from $69.27 billion in October 2025 to $89.99 billion. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters that India had "not achieved USD 89.99 billion ever till now in any month".

Here is how the two halves add up:

  • Goods sold abroad: $49.47 billion, up from $34.11 billion a year earlier. Mr Agrawal called it the highest monthly value ever, with growth of 45.06%, the fastest in five years.
  • Services sold abroad: an estimated $40.51 billion, up from $35.17 billion. The October services number is still an estimate, because the RBI's final data comes later.

Add them: $49.47 billion plus $40.51 billion makes $89.99 billion after rounding.

Mr Agrawal also said the rise was wide. According to The Economic Times, 43 of India's top 50 export markets bought more from India than a year earlier.

So why is there a gap?

A trade deficit is what you get when you spend more than you earn. Say you earn Rs 500 a month selling samosas, but you spend Rs 900 on oil, flour and potatoes from other sellers. Your gap is Rs 400.

For goods alone, India spent far more than it earned in October. It bought goods worth $89.35 billion, up from $76.69 billion in October 2025. Business Standard reported that this was a record for imports of goods in a single month.

Now do the sum: $89.35 billion bought minus $49.47 billion sold leaves a gap of $39.88 billion. In September 2026 the same gap was $30.21 billion. October's gap was the highest in 12 months, but still smaller than the $42.58 billion gap of October 2025.

The good news hidden inside

India earns well from services, like software, consulting and support work. In October, services brought in about $40.51 billion and cost about $20.72 billion. That left a services surplus of around $19.79 billion, Business Standard said.

This surplus fills a big part of the hole on goods. Put goods and services together, and the total trade deficit was $20.09 billion in October 2026. A year earlier, it was $25.15 billion. So the overall gap actually shrank.

Why oil prices pushed both numbers up

India buys most of its crude oil from other countries. When oil gets costlier, the import bill grows, even if the same number of barrels arrive. In October, the price of the Indian basket of crude oil climbed to $119.91 a barrel, an over 14-year high, Business Standard reported. Imports of crude oil jumped 54% to $22.82 billion.

But oil also helps on the selling side. Indian refineries turn crude into diesel, petrol and jet fuel, and sell some of it abroad. The ministry's data shows that petroleum products sold abroad rose 140.21%, from $3.70 billion to $8.89 billion. Mr Agrawal said this came both from higher prices and from more demand for refined fuel from India.

Think of a chai stall. If milk gets costlier, the stall pays more for milk. If it also sells milk sweets, it can charge more for those too. Both bills go up.

The Global Trade Research Initiative, a think tank, said a big part of the jump in dollar value came from higher world prices for commodities, not only from selling more, ET reported.

What happened with gold?

Gold can swing the import bill a lot. In October 2026, gold imports fell nearly 63% from a year earlier to $5.51 billion, Business Standard reported. Compared with September, though, gold imports nearly tripled from $1.8 billion, according to ET.

Price matters here too. The bill for gold equals the amount bought times the price. The World Gold Council said world gold prices fell sharply in September and stayed in a narrow range in October, and that the lower prices were helping festive demand.

Other big movers

  • Electronics: India sold electronic goods worth $6.64 billion, up from $4.08 billion, a rise of 62.70%, the ministry said. India also bought electronic goods worth $14.32 billion, nearly 50% more, partly to make products for sale abroad.
  • Engineering goods: sales abroad grew 36.01% to $12.74 billion.
  • The US stayed India's top buyer, taking goods worth $8.72 billion, while China stayed the top seller to India at $16.26 billion.

Why should a young Indian care?

More selling abroad usually means more work in factories, ports and offices that serve foreign buyers. But a big goods gap means India needs lots of dollars to pay for oil, gold and parts. Costly imported fuel can also push up prices at home. The RBI has warned that higher energy and transport costs could raise costs for businesses, ET reported.

From April to October 2026, India's total exports reached an estimated $568.84 billion, up 16.66%. Mr Agrawal said he was "very optimistic" the growth would continue towards the $1 trillion export goal.
